entry: Women's professional basketball league in North America. Founded on April 24, 1996, as the women's counterpart to the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]], it began play in 1997. It now has 15 teams, 14 in the United States and one in [[Canada]], and is scheduled to expand to 18. The league is headquartered in [[New York City]]. Its regular season runs from May to September, with 44 games per team. The top eight teams qualify for the playoffs, which end with the finals in November.

Professional [[Association football|association football]] league and the highest level of women's football in England. Established by the Football Association in 2010, it was inaugurated in 2011 with eight teams and now has 14 fully professional clubs. The league has operated as a winter competition, from September to May, since 2017–18. The top three finishers qualify for the [[UEFA]] Women's Champions League. Chelsea has won the title eight times and Arsenal three, while Liverpool and Manchester City have two titles each. Manchester City won its second title in the 2025–26 season.

Branch of historical study concerned with the role of women in history. It examines the growth of [[Women's rights|women's rights]], women's achievements, and the effects of historical events on women. Its premise is that traditional histories minimized or ignored women's contributions, which makes the field a form of historical revisionism. Scholars in the United States and Britain, led by second-wave feminist historians, developed it as an academic discipline in the mid-1970s. Work has moved from recovering lost stories toward integrating women's experiences into mainstream narratives. Some critics argue that the field overemphasizes oppression and underplays women's agency. Notable subjects include [[Cleopatra]], [[Joan of Arc]], [[Marie Curie]], [[Jane Austen]], [[Harriet Tubman]], and [[Malala Yousafzai]].

Rights and entitlements claimed for women and girls worldwide. They formed the basis of the women's rights movement of the 19th century and of later feminist movements. Some countries enshrine these rights in law, while others ignore or suppress them. Issues commonly associated with them include bodily integrity, freedom from sexual violence, voting, holding public office, entering legal contracts, equal rights in family law, equal pay, reproductive rights, owning property, and education. Legal status has varied widely: in ancient [[Sumer]], women could buy, own, sell, and inherit property, while in [[Classical Athens]] women had no legal personhood. In the United States, the 19th Amendment (1920) secured women's federal voting rights. Researchers disagree about the causes of remaining gaps in pay and leadership; some emphasize discrimination, while others point to biological differences in interests and preferences.

Participation of women and girls in sport, fitness, and exercise, which has existed throughout history. Until about 1870, women's physical activity was largely informal and recreational, with few formal rules. Women's sport later developed amateur and professional levels, mainly in developed countries. Professional women's sport rarely provides a livable income, except in a few cases such as [[Tennis|women's professional tennis]]. Female participation grew in the late 20th century but remains smaller than male participation. Very few sports have been invented by women; [[Netball]] is one example. In the United States, the 1972 enactment of Title IX, which prohibits sex discrimination in federally funded education, helped drive a surge in women's collegiate sports. Debate continues over transgender women's inclusion in female categories, and some studies cited in that debate report retained strength advantages.

Legal right of women to vote in elections. The first national grant of women's suffrage came in 1893 in the self-governing British colony of New Zealand. By the interwar period most major Western powers had followed, including Canada (1917), Germany (1918), Austria and the Netherlands (1919), the [[United States]] (1920), and the [[United Kingdom]] (1928). France did not grant women the vote until 1944, and [[Switzerland]] allowed women to vote at the federal level only in 1971. Suffrage spread in two waves: 1893–1930, mainly in English-speaking and Scandinavian countries, and 1930–1970, across most of Latin America and much of sub-Saharan Africa. After World War II the United Nations encouraged women's suffrage, and the 1979 Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination Against Women names it a basic right.

Superheroine appearing in American comic books published by [[DC Comics]]. She first appeared in *All Star Comics* #8 in October 1941 and was created by psychologist William Moulton Marston, who wrote under the pen name Charles Moulton, and artist Harry G. Peter. Marston's wife, Elizabeth, and their partner, Olive Byrne, are credited as inspirations for her appearance. An Amazon princess from the island of Themyscira, she is known there as Princess Diana. In her original origin story, her mother, Queen Hippolyta, sculpted her from clay, and Greek goddesses gave her powers. Early stories, created during [[World War II]], pitted her against Axis forces and supervillains, while later stories drew more on [[Greek mythology]]. Many stories showed her freeing herself from bondage, and she has been widely adapted in film and television.

Shanghai-born Hong Kong filmmaker who emigrated as a child. He began as a screenwriter for soap operas before directing his debut, the crime drama *As Tears Go By* (1988). His films, often built on nonlinear narratives and atmospheric music, are known for saturated colors. *Chungking Express* (1994) brought him international prominence, and *Happy Together* (1997) won him Best Director at the [[Cannes Film Festival]]. *In the Mood for Love* (2000) established his trademark style. Later works include *2046* (2004) and *The Grandmaster* (2013), a biopic of Ip Man. An auteur of Hong Kong cinema, he often appears at international film festivals.

Terrestrial [[Crustacean|crustacean]] of the suborder Oniscidea, also called a sowbug, slater, or pillbug. The name refers to its frequent presence in old wood and to the [[Louse|louse]], although woodlice are neither parasitic nor [[Insect|insects]]. They are detritivores that break down leaf litter and contribute to humus formation, and some species re-ingest their feces to gain nutrients. Woodlice have seven pairs of jointed legs and breathe through pleopods adapted for respiration. Females carry eggs in a marsupium, and some species roll into a ball when threatened. Their exoskeletons lose water easily, so they hide under logs and rocks. The oldest known fossils date from the mid-[[Cretaceous]] period, about 100 million years ago. Woodlice live on every continent except [[Antarctica]] and are popular pets.

Family of birds (Picidae) that also includes piculets, wrynecks, and sapsuckers. Woodpeckers are found worldwide except in [[Australia]], [[New Guinea]], [[New Zealand]], [[Madagascar]], and the polar regions. Most live in [[Forest|forests]] or woodlands, though some inhabit deserts and rocky hillsides. They peck trunks and branches to find [[Insect|insect]] prey and drum on trees to communicate. Most nest and roost in holes they excavate in trees, and abandoned holes benefit other cavity-nesting birds. The family includes about 240 species in 35 genera, ranging from the bar-breasted piculet, 7.5 cm long, to species over 50 cm. Almost 20 species are threatened by habitat loss. The ivory-billed and imperial woodpeckers are generally considered extinct, though that status is not universally accepted.

Democratic 28th president of the United States (1913–21). A former president of [[Princeton University]], he was governor of New Jersey before winning the presidency. In the 1912 election he defeated the Republican incumbent [[William Howard Taft]] and the third-party candidate [[Theodore Roosevelt]]. His first term produced the Revenue Act of 1913, which began the modern income tax, and the Federal Reserve Act. He led the United States into [[World War I]] in 1917 and championed the [[League of Nations]], which was included in the [[Treaty of Versailles]], but the Senate did not ratify the treaty. A stroke in 1919 left him incapacitated for the rest of his term. Historians criticize his support for racial segregation in federal offices, although many still rank him an above-average president.

Music festival held August 15–18, 1969, on a dairy farm in Bethel, New York. Billed as "an Aquarian Exposition: 3 Days of Peace & Music," it drew more than 460,000 people, and 32 acts performed despite overcast skies and sporadic rain. It became the peak musical event of the 1960s counterculture. A 1970 documentary and a [[Joni Mitchell]] song that became a hit for Crosby, Stills, Nash & Young reinforced its legacy. In 2004, *Rolling Stone* ranked it 19th among the 50 moments that changed rock and roll. The site was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2017.

Family of musical wind instruments, including the [[Flute|flute]], [[Clarinet|clarinet]], oboe, bassoon, and [[Saxophone|saxophone]]. Woodwinds produce sound in one of two ways: flutes split an air stream on a sharp edge, while reed instruments vibrate one or two reeds. Despite the name, woodwinds need not be made of wood. Modern concert flutes are usually made of metal alloys containing nickel, silver, copper, or gold, and some woodwinds, especially [[Ocarina|ocarinas]], are made of earthen materials. The saxophone is made of brass but counts as a woodwind because it requires a reed. Double-reed instruments may have originated in the middle to late [[Neolithic]] period.

Skill of making items from [[Wood|wood]], including cabinetry, furniture making, wood carving, joinery, [[Carpentry|carpentry]], and woodturning. Among the earliest woodworking finds are notched, shaped sticks from Kalambo Falls in southern Africa, dating to around 476,000 years ago. In [[Ancient Egypt]], woodworkers used mortise and tenon joints from the Predynastic period and tools of copper and, after 2000 BC, bronze. Many Egyptian chairs, stools, tables, and beds have been preserved. In ancient Rome, [[Vitruvius]] devoted a chapter of *De architectura* to timber. Woodworking today ranges from artisanal workshop craft to mechanized production, which emerged with the Industrial Revolution. Carpentry, by contrast, focuses on on-site structural construction.

American filmmaker, actor, and writer. After starting as a comedy writer and stand-up performer in Greenwich Village, Allen directed the slapstick comedies *Take the Money and Run* (1969) and *Sleeper* (1973). His romantic comedy-drama *Annie Hall* (1977), starring [[Diane Keaton]], won four [[Academy Awards]]. He has since made a film almost every year, many of them set in New York City. He collaborated with actress [[Mia Farrow]] on 13 films between 1980 and 1992. In 1992 Farrow publicly accused Allen of sexually abusing their adopted daughter. Allen denied the allegation and was never charged with a crime. He married Soon-Yi Previn in 1997.

American folk singer-songwriter whose work focused on socialism and anti-fascism. Guthrie wrote hundreds of songs, including the 1940 album *Dust Bowl Ballads* and "This Land Is Your Land," written in 1940 as a response to Irving Berlin's "God Bless America." His songs influenced [[Bob Dylan]], [[Johnny Cash]], [[Bruce Springsteen]], and many later musicians. He was associated with United States communist groups, although there is no evidence that he was a member of one. He often displayed the message "This machine kills fascists" on his guitar. He died in 1967 from complications of [[Huntington's disease]], inherited from his mother. Many of his recordings are archived in the [[Library of Congress]].

American actor. He is known for playing bartender Woody Boyd on the [[NBC]] sitcom *Cheers* (1985–93), a role that won him a Primetime Emmy Award in 1989. He received Academy Award nominations for Best Actor in *The People vs. Larry Flynt* (1996) and for Best Supporting Actor in *The Messenger* (2009) and *Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri* (2017). His other films include *White Men Can't Jump* (1992), *No Country for Old Men* (2007), and *Zombieland* (2009). He played Haymitch Abernathy in the *Hunger Games* series. He has advocated for [[Cannabis|cannabis]] legalization.

Textile fiber obtained mainly from [[Sheep|sheep]] and also from [[Goat|goats]], [[Rabbit|rabbits]], and camelids. Wool is an animal fiber made mostly of [[Protein|protein]], chiefly keratin, with about 2–3% lipids. This makes it chemically distinct from plant fibers such as cotton, which is mainly cellulose, and akin to silk. Its natural crimp and surface scales help fibers cling together during spinning and felting. Crimp also gives wool fabric bulk, so it holds air that retains heat. A fine wool such as [[Merino]] may have up to 40 crimps per centimeter (100 per inch). Wet wool is generally weaker than dry wool. After collection, wool is cleaned and carded or combed before being made into yarn, felt, insulation, or fertilizer.

Extinct species of mammoth that lived from the Middle Pleistocene into the Holocene. Its closest living relative is the [[Asian elephant]]. It was covered in fur, with small ears and a short tail that reduced frostbite and heat loss. Its long, curved tusks were used for foraging and fighting. It lived on the mammoth steppe of northern Eurasia and North America and was hunted by early humans. The last mainland populations in [[Siberia]] persisted until about 10,000 years ago, and isolated island populations survived until about 4,000 years ago. Its genome, completed in 2015, prompted discussion of reviving the species.

City in central [[Massachusetts]], U.S., and seat of Worcester County (pop., 2020: 206,518). Named after Worcester, England, it is known as the "Heart of the Commonwealth." It was founded as a town in 1722 and incorporated as a city in 1848. Its 19th-century industries, including textiles and wire, grew with the Blackstone Canal and railways. Manufacturing declined after World War II, but higher education, medicine, and biotechnology began to reverse the decline in the 1990s. Eight colleges and universities include the College of the Holy Cross and Worcester Polytechnic Institute. Some 22% of residents were born outside the United States.

Fermented [[Condiment|condiment]] invented by the [[Pharmacist|pharmacists]] John Wheeley Lea and William Henry Perrins in Worcester, England, in the first half of the 19th century. The Lea & Perrins brand, the first to bear the Worcestershire name, was commercialized in 1837. A court ruling in 1876 held that the name had become generic. Typical ingredients include vinegar, salt, molasses or sugar, garlic, onions, soy sauce, and anchovies or fish sauce. The company's claim that a "Lord Sandys" brought the recipe from India is not supported by historical records. The sauce flavors steaks and cocktails such as the [[Cocktail|Bloody Mary]] and the [[Caesar salad]].

Device or computer program for the input, editing, formatting, and output of text. Early word processors were standalone machines, but most are now software running on [[Personal computer|personal computers]] and [[Smartphone|smartphones]]. Mechanical forerunners include a machine for transcribing letters patented in 1714 by Henry Mill, and the first recognizable typewriter, created by Christopher Latham Sholes in the late 19th century. The term "word processing" entered American offices in the early 1970s. The Data Secretary, introduced in 1971, was an early standalone computerized word processor. Software programs proliferated in the late 1970s, and [[Microsoft Word]] was launched in 1983. Google Docs, launched in 2006, added real-time collaboration in a web browser.

Energy transferred to or from an object by a [[Force|force]] acting along a displacement. For a constant force aligned with the motion, work equals the force multiplied by the distance traveled; in general it depends on the [[Angle|angle]] between the two vectors. Work is positive when the force has a component in the direction of displacement and negative when it opposes the displacement. A dropped ball gains positive work from gravity, while a thrown ball has negative work. Work is a scalar measured in [[Joule|joules]] in the [[International System of Units]]. The term was introduced in the late 1820s by French scientists Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis and Jean-Victor Poncelet. Earlier, [[Galileo Galilei|Galileo]] had shown that [[Simple machine|simple machines]] transform energy rather than create it.

Ruling party of [[North Korea]]. Founded in 1949 by a merger of the North and South Korean workers' parties, it is the oldest active party in Korea and controls the [[Korean People's Army]]. Kim Il Sung led it when he launched the [[Korean War]] in 1950. Kim Jong Il succeeded him in 1994 and Kim Jong Un in 2011. Officially a communist party, it is guided by Kimilsungism–Kimjongilism and the ideology of [[Juche]]. In 2023 it abandoned its goal of Korean reunification. The party is banned in South Korea and sanctioned by the [[United Nations]], the [[European Union]], Australia, and the [[United States]].

Social class of people who depend on wages or salaries for their livelihood. In the United States the term usually covers blue-collar and pink-collar workers, or those whose income falls below the middle class. Socialists define it more broadly, to include all who must sell their labor to live. [[Karl Marx]] called this group the proletariat and, with [[Friedrich Engels]], argued in *The Communist Manifesto* that the working class would displace capitalism. Other definitions rely on income, education, or self-identification. The class emerged during the Industrial Revolution, as [[Enclosure|enclosure]] displaced smallholders and artisans. Debates continue over whether the class is shrinking through educational expansion and growth in service jobs.
